details:
**Quetzalcoatl**
The "Feathered Serpent," one of the most important Aztec gods, associated with wind, learning, and creation, and sometimes described as a white god. Tricked by his rival Tezcatlipoca into getting drunk and sleeping with his sister, he leaves in shame (in some versions on a raft of serpents) or burns himself and becomes the morning star (Venus).

**Huitzilopochtli**
The Aztec god of war and the sun, whose name means "Hummingbird of the South" or "Left-Handed Hummingbird." He was the patron of the Mexica, and the Aztecs believed they had to offer him human sacrifices, especially hearts and blood, to keep the sun strong and moving across the sky.

**Coatlicue and the ball of feathers**
Huitzilopochtli's mother Coatlicue ("Serpent Skirt") becomes pregnant when a ball of feathers falls into her clothing while she sweeps on Coatepec (Snake Mountain). Her daughter Coyolxauhqui and her 400 sons, the Centzon Huitznahua, try to kill her for the shameful pregnancy, but Huitzilopochtli is born fully armed and kills them, dismembering his sister, whose head becomes the moon.

**Tezcatlipoca**
The "Smoking Mirror," a dark, powerful god of night, sorcery, and fate and the arch-rival of Quetzalcoatl. He is shown with an obsidian mirror in place of the foot he lost to the earth monster Cipactli.

**Cipactli and the creation of the earth**
A primordial crocodile-like monster of the waters. Tezcatlipoca uses his own foot as bait to catch it, losing the foot in the process, and he and Quetzalcoatl tear the monster apart to make the earth and the heavens. The Aztecs believed in thirteen heavens and nine underworld levels.

**The Five Suns**
Aztec cosmology holds that the world has been created and destroyed four times, with each age ruled by a different sun. The earlier ages were ended by jaguars, wind, a rain of fire, and a flood (whose people turned into fish), and the present age is the Fifth Sun, Nahui Ollin ("Four Movement"), which is destined to end in earthquakes. In the first age, the one-footed Tezcatlipoca was a dim, half-sized sun until Quetzalcoatl knocked him out of the sky with a club.

**Nanahuatzin and the rabbit in the moon**
To create the Fifth Sun the gods gather at Teotihuacan, where the humble, sore-covered god Nanahuatzin leaps into a bonfire and becomes the sun. The proud Tecciztecatl jumps in second and also becomes a sun, so the gods throw a rabbit at his face to dim him, making him the moon and leaving the image of a rabbit on it.

**Mictlan and the bones of humanity**
Mictlan is the Aztec underworld, ruled by Mictlantecuhtli. To create the humans of the Fifth Sun, Quetzalcoatl goes down to Mictlan to steal the bones of earlier humans. The goddess Cihuacoatl grinds the bones into powder, and Quetzalcoatl sheds his own blood on them to bring the new people to life.

**Xolotl**
A dog-headed god of death, lightning, and monsters, often called Quetzalcoatl's twin. He accompanies Quetzalcoatl to Mictlan, guides the dead to the underworld, and is linked to Venus as the evening star.

**Templo Mayor and Tenochtitlan**
The Templo Mayor was the great pyramid at the center of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan (modern Mexico City). It had twin temples on top, one dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and one to the rain god Tlaloc, and it was the sacred center of Aztec religion.

**Eagle on a cactus eating a snake**
Huitzilopochtli tells the wandering Mexica to settle where they see an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a snake. They see this sign on an island in Lake Texcoco and found Tenochtitlan there, and the image appears on the modern Mexican flag.

**Tlaloc**
The Aztec rain and fertility god, honored with child sacrifices since children's tears were thought to bring rain. He rules Tlalocan, a paradise of eternal springtime. When he was the third sun, Tezcatlipoca stole his wife Xochiquetzal, and in his grief he rained fire on the world and destroyed it.

**Xipe Totec**
"Our Lord the Flayed One," an Aztec god of agriculture, spring, and renewal. His priests wore the flayed skins of sacrificial victims, and he was said to have flayed himself to give food to humanity, symbolizing a seed shedding its husk.

**New Fire Ceremony**
A ritual held every 52 years when the Aztec calendar cycle ended. All fires were put out, and priests on a hill near Tenochtitlan watched for the stars to keep moving; then a new fire was kindled in the chest of a sacrificed victim and spread throughout the land, ensuring the world would go on.

**Teotihuacan and Hernan Cortes**
Teotihuacan is an older ruined city whose name, given by the Aztecs, means "city of the gods" in Nahuatl, the Aztec language. The Aztec Empire fell to the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes in 1521, and a famous (but disputed) story says the emperor Moctezuma II believed Cortes was the returning Quetzalcoatl.
